title: Landscape of incompressible crystals of hard-core bosons on the square-kagome lattice
abstract: We investigate a hard-core boson model on the square-kagome lattice using hierarchical mean-field theory beyond the conventional unit-cell description. We show that the conventional description of the square-kagome lattice based on its smallest unit cell does not fully capture the hierarchy of incompressible states supported by the lattice, but only captures the two compact-localized-state-based phases at densities $5/6$ and $2/3$. Within our approach, we reproduce these previously established phases and uncover additional incompressible states enabled by enlarging the variational cluster. Among these, the $ρ=3/4$ phase is found to be particularly robust, which, through the Matsubara-Matsuda mapping, corresponds to a half-magnetization plateau in the spin-$1/2$ XXZ model. We further apply our approach to two experimentally relevant square-kagome compounds using exchange parameters obtained from first-principles calculations. The calculated magnetization processes are in good agreement with available experimental results and predict additional plateau structures in these materials.
summary: This work explores the complex ground state structure of hard-core bosons on the square-kagome lattice using an advanced hierarchical mean-field theory. By systematically enlarging the variational cluster, the authors uncover a hierarchy of previously unknown incompressible phases, including a robust $\rho=3/4$ state. These theoretical findings are validated by predicting additional magnetization plateaus in real superconducting materials.
main_problem: The study investigates the complex landscape of incompressible crystal states supported by hard-core bosons on the square-kagome lattice (SKL), aiming to find phases beyond those predicted by simple unit-cell descriptions.
main_result: By employing hierarchical mean-field theory with larger variational clusters, the authors discovered additional robust incompressible phases, notably at density $\rho=3/4$, which map to half-magnetization plateaus in related spin models.
method: The primary method is Hierarchical Mean-Field Theory (HMFT), which systematically increases the size of the variational cluster beyond conventional limits to capture richer correlation effects.
model_or_system: The system is a hard-core boson model on the SKL, mathematically mapped onto an effective spin-$1/2$ XXZ model via the Matsubara-Matsuda transformation. The analysis involves comparing theoretical predictions with magnetization data from real cuprate compounds.
key_observables: Incompressible crystal densities ($\rho$), magnetization plateaus ($m/m_s$), and local particle densities ($n_i$).
important_parameters: Boson hopping ($t$), interaction strength ($V$), chemical potential ($\mu$), and the size of the variational cluster (12-site up to 24-site).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on mapping the bosonic system to a spin model, and the HMFT approach approximates inter-cluster correlations while treating intra-cluster physics exactly.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the geometries of compact localized states (CLS) and show phase diagrams derived from calculations using 12-site and 24-site clusters, mapping out incompressible regions.
paper_structure: The paper first introduces the model and HMFT. It then demonstrates that increasing cluster size reveals new incompressible phases beyond the conventional two known phases ($\rho=5/6$ and $\rho=2/3$). Finally, it applies this framework to predict magnetization plateaus in specific, experimentally relevant superconducting compounds.
why_interesting: The use of a highly correlated lattice model (SKL) combined with advanced mean-field techniques to predict novel quantum phases and compare them directly against experimental magnetic measurements makes this highly relevant for condensed matter theorists studying strongly interacting quantum magnets.

FIG. 2. Cluster geometries used in the hierarchical mean-field calculations. (a) The 12-site cluster, which represents the smallest cluster considered in this work. (b) The 24-site cluster (Setup 1), chosen to accommodate the different localized structures discussed in the text. (c) The alternative 24-site cluster (Setup 2), which contains the same number of sites as Setup 1 but preserves the fourfold rotational symmetry around the centers of the octagonal plaquettes.

FIG. 3. Ground-state phase diagrams obtained from cluster mean-field theory. (a) Phase diagram obtained using the 12-site cluster. The blue regions denote compressible phases with continuously varying density, while the other regions correspond to incompressible phases. The incompressible plateaus appear at ρ = 1/2, 2/3, 3/4, and 5/6. (b) Phase diagram obtained using the 24-site cluster (Setup 1). The overall phase diagram is in qualitative agreement with the 12-site result, while the enlarged cluster stabilizes additional incompressible phases at ρ = 13/24 and ρ = 19/24.

FIG. 4. Comparison of the phase diagram obtained using the alternative 24-site cluster (Setup 2) and the corresponding local observables. (a) Upper part of the phase diagram (µ′ ≥0.4) calculated using Setup 2. The lower-density region is qualitatively identical to the result obtained from Setup 1 and is not shown. Compared with Setup 1, the ρ = 19/24 incompressible phase becomes smaller, while an additional incompressible phase emerges at ρ = 17/24, located between the ρ = 2/3 and ρ = 3/4 plateaus. FIG. 5. Magnetic properties of square-kagome compounds. (a) Exchange network and calculated magnetization curve of KCu6AlBiO4(SO4)5Cl using the 24-site Setup 2. The calculated results show good agreement with available experimental data, reproducing the observed m/ms = 1/3 and 2/3 plateaus and predicting additional plateau structures, with the lowest-field plateau appearing at m/ms = 1/4. The inset shows the local density and hopping expectation values of the m/ms = 1/4 plateau. (b) Exchange network and calculated magnetization curve of Na6Cu7BiO4(PO)4Cl3. The system exhibits plateaus at m/ms = 1/3 and 5/6, with a shoulder near m/ms = 2/3.
